Java collections: contracts and what the documentation actually promises

This reference supports the factual review of the existing Java collections material. Each claim below is tied to wording in the Java SE API documentation; anything not stated there is an implementation detail.

## equals and hashCode

- Equal objects must have equal hash codes. Override both together. A class used as a `HashMap` key or `HashSet` element with only `equals` overridden will not be found reliably.
- Records (Java 16+) generate both from their components. Arrays do not override `equals`; use `Arrays.equals`/`Arrays.hashCode`, or wrap in a `List`.
- Mutating a field that participates in `hashCode` while the object is in a hash collection makes it unreachable by lookup.

## Comparable and Comparator

- `compareTo` and `compare` must be antisymmetric and transitive. The documentation strongly recommends, but does not require, consistency with `equals`. A `TreeSet` or `TreeMap` uses only the comparator, so two objects that compare as 0 are treated as duplicates even if `equals` says otherwise.
- `(a, b) -> a - b` can overflow for large or negative ints. Use `Integer.compare(a, b)` or `Comparator.comparingInt(...)`.
- `Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...).reversed()` builds compound orders; `reversed()` applies to the whole chain built so far.
- `Collections.sort` and `List.sort` for objects are stable (documented); `Arrays.sort` for primitives is a dual-pivot quicksort and has no stability concept for primitives.

## What the complexity documentation says

- `HashMap`: "constant-time performance for the basic operations (get and put), assuming the hash function disperses the elements properly". Since Java 8 the implementation converts large buckets of `Comparable` keys into trees, but that is an implementation note, not an API guarantee.
- `TreeMap`: guaranteed log(n) time for `containsKey`, `get`, `put` and `remove` (red-black tree).
- `PriorityQueue`: O(log n) for `offer`, `poll`, `remove()` and `add`; linear time for `remove(Object)` and `contains`; constant time for `peek`, `element` and `size`. Its iterator does not traverse in priority order. It is a min-heap by natural order or the supplied comparator.
- `ArrayList`: `get`/`set` constant time, `add` amortized constant time; `add(0, x)` and `remove(0)` are linear. `ArrayDeque` is the documented recommendation for stacks and queues and is likely faster than `Stack` and `LinkedList`; it rejects `null`.
- `LinkedList.get(i)` walks the list, linear in the distance from the nearer end.

## Iteration and ConcurrentModificationException

The iterators of the standard non-concurrent collections are fail-fast on a best-effort basis: structural modification during iteration, other than through the iterator's own `remove`, usually throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. The documentation explicitly says this cannot be guaranteed, so code must not rely on the exception. Use `iterator.remove()`, `removeIf`, or collect changes and apply them afterwards.

## Ordering of hash collections

`HashMap` and `HashSet` make no guarantees about iteration order, and the order can change over time. `LinkedHashMap`/`LinkedHashSet` keep insertion order (or access order for `LinkedHashMap` with the right constructor); `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` keep sorted order. Java 21 added `SequencedCollection` and `SequencedMap` interfaces with `getFirst`, `getLast`, `reversed` and related methods.

## Unmodifiable views

`List.of`, `Set.of` and `Map.of` (Java 9+) are unmodifiable and reject `null`; `Set.of` and `Map.of` also reject duplicates and have unspecified iteration order. `Collections.unmodifiableList` is a read-only view of a list that can still change underneath.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Your `TreeSet` lost an element. What does your comparator return for that element and the one it collided with?
- Which collection does your queue use, and what does removing from the front cost there?
- Does your code depend on the order a `HashMap` iterates in?

Java CompletableFuture

`CompletableFuture<T>` represents a result that will be available later and lets you chain dependent steps without blocking.

## Starting work and choosing an executor

- `supplyAsync(supplier)` and `runAsync(runnable)` without an executor run on `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` (unless its parallelism is too low, in which case a new thread per task is used). The common pool is shared by the whole JVM, including parallel streams, so long blocking calls there starve other work.
- Pass your own `Executor` for blocking I/O: `supplyAsync(() -> load(id), ioExecutor)`. In Java 21, a virtual-thread-per-task executor is a common choice for blocking calls.

## Composing

- `thenApply(fn)` transforms the result (like `map`).
- `thenCompose(fn)` chains a step that itself returns a `CompletionStage` (like `flatMap`). Using `thenApply` there produces a nested `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>`.
- `thenCombine(other, fn)` waits for two independent futures.
- `allOf(...)` completes when all complete and returns `CompletableFuture<Void>`; read each result afterwards with `join()`. `anyOf(...)` completes with the first result, typed as `Object`.
- Non-`Async` variants may run the next step on the thread that completed the previous stage, or on the caller's thread if it is already complete. The `...Async` variants run it on the default or given executor.

## Errors

If a stage throws, dependent stages are skipped and complete exceptionally, wrapping the cause in a `CompletionException`.

- `exceptionally(fn)` recovers with a value; `exceptionallyCompose` (Java 12+) recovers with another stage.
- `handle((value, error) -> ...)` sees both outcomes and returns a new value.
- `whenComplete` observes both outcomes without changing the result (unless it throws).
- `join()` throws an unchecked `CompletionException`; `get()` throws checked `ExecutionException` and `InterruptedException`. Unwrap with `getCause()` to see the original exception.

A future whose failure is never observed fails silently. End every chain with handling or a `join` somewhere.

## Timeouts and cancellation

`orTimeout(d, unit)` completes exceptionally with `TimeoutException`; `completeOnTimeout(value, d, unit)` substitutes a value (both Java 9+). `cancel(true)` on a `CompletableFuture` completes it with `CancellationException` but, as the documentation states, does not interrupt the computation that would have completed it. Long-running suppliers need their own cancellation check.

## When not to use it

For a small number of sequential blocking calls, plain code on a virtual thread is often clearer. Parallelizing a CPU-bound DSA computation with many tiny futures usually adds overhead; measure before and after.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Which thread runs this `thenApply` step, and does it do blocking work?
- Your chain returned a nested future. Which composition method fits a step that returns a future?
- Where in this chain would a failure from the first step be noticed?

Java generics, wildcards and type erasure

## Generic types are invariant

`List<Integer>` is not a subtype of `List<Number>`, even though `Integer` is a subtype of `Number`. If it were, code could add a `Double` to a list of integers. Arrays are different: `Integer[]` is a subtype of `Number[]`, and storing a `Double` into it compiles but throws `ArrayStoreException` at run time.

## Wildcards express variance at the use site

- `List<? extends Number>` accepts a list of `Number` or any subtype. You can read elements as `Number`, but you cannot add anything except `null`, because the actual element type is unknown.
- `List<? super Integer>` accepts a list of `Integer` or any supertype. You can add `Integer` values, but reading gives only `Object`.
- `List<?>` accepts a list of anything; reads give `Object`.

The guideline often summarized as PECS ("producer extends, consumer super"): use `? extends T` for parameters the method reads from and `? super T` for parameters it writes to. `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` and `Comparator<? super T>` parameters in the sorting APIs follow it. That is why a `Comparator<Object>` or `Comparator<Number>` can sort a `List<Integer>`.

## Bounded type parameters

`<T extends Comparable<? super T>> void sort(List<T> list)` is the shape used by `Collections.sort`. The `? super T` allows types whose `compareTo` is inherited from a superclass, such as `java.sql.Timestamp` comparing as `java.util.Date`. Multiple bounds use `&`: `<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>`.

## Type erasure

Generic type arguments are checked by the compiler and then erased: at run time a `List<String>` and a `List<Integer>` are both `List`. Consequences:

- `new T()`, `new T[n]`, `instanceof List<String>` and `T.class` do not compile. Pass a `Class<T>`, a `Supplier<T>` or an `IntFunction<T[]>` when the type is needed at run time.
- Generic arrays such as `List<Integer>[]` cannot be created directly; `new ArrayList[n]` with an unchecked cast compiles with a warning. A `List<List<Integer>>` is usually the better adjacency structure.
- Overloads that differ only by type argument (`f(List<String>)` and `f(List<Integer>)`) clash after erasure.
- Raw types (`List` without `<>`) disable checking and produce "unchecked" warnings. Heap pollution from raw types surfaces later as `ClassCastException` far from the cause.

## Primitives

Type arguments must be reference types. `List<int>` does not compile; `List<Integer>` boxes each value. Boxing costs memory and time, and `Integer` comparison with `==` compares references: values in the small cached range (at least -128 to 127) may compare equal by identity while larger ones usually do not. Use `.equals` or unbox. Primitive arrays (`int[]`) or primitive streams (`IntStream`) avoid boxing.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Why does the compiler reject adding an `Integer` to a `List<? extends Number>`?
- Your comparator is declared for a supertype. Which wildcard lets the sort method accept it?
- Two `Integer` values print the same number but `==` says false. What is `==` comparing?

Java JDBC basics

JDBC is the standard Java API for relational databases (`java.sql`). A vendor driver on the classpath implements it. Frameworks such as Spring's `JdbcTemplate`, JPA/Hibernate and jOOQ are built on top of it.

## Getting a connection

- `DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password)` opens a new physical connection each time. JDBC 4 drivers register automatically; `Class.forName(...)` is no longer needed.
- Applications usually obtain connections from a `DataSource` backed by a connection pool (for example HikariCP). Closing a pooled connection returns it to the pool.
- Credentials belong in configuration, not in source code.

## Close everything with try-with-resources

`Connection`, `Statement`/`PreparedStatement` and `ResultSet` are `AutoCloseable`. Resources declared in one `try (...)` are closed in reverse order, even when an exception is thrown. Leaking connections exhausts the pool and makes the application hang under load. See the resource lifetime starter reference.

```java
try (Connection c = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = ?")) {
    ps.setString(1, email);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        while (rs.next()) { /* rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("name") */ }
    }
}
```

## Always use parameters

Building SQL by string concatenation with user input allows SQL injection. `PreparedStatement` placeholders (`?`) send values separately from the SQL text. Placeholders work for values only; table or column names cannot be parameterized and must come from an allowlist.

Parameter and column indexes start at 1. `rs.getInt` returns 0 for SQL `NULL`; call `rs.wasNull()` or use `getObject(i, Integer.class)` to tell them apart.

## Transactions

Connections start in auto-commit mode: each statement commits immediately. For several statements that must succeed or fail together:

1. `c.setAutoCommit(false)`
2. execute the statements
3. `c.commit()`, or `c.rollback()` in a catch block

Restore auto-commit (or rely on the pool resetting it) before the connection is reused. The isolation level (`setTransactionIsolation`) and how strictly it is enforced depend on the database.

## Batching and large results

`addBatch` / `executeBatch` sends many parameter sets at once. For large result sets, `setFetchSize` is a hint to the driver; whether rows are streamed depends on the driver and sometimes on extra settings.

## Errors

`SQLException` carries `getSQLState()` (standardized classes such as `23` for integrity constraint violations) and `getErrorCode()` (vendor-specific). Chained exceptions are available through `getNextException()` and iteration over the exception.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Where is this connection closed if the query throws?
- How would a value containing a single quote change this concatenated SQL?
- If the second insert fails, what has already been committed?

Java unit testing with JUnit 5

JUnit 5 consists of the JUnit Platform (launcher and engines), JUnit Jupiter (the programming model below) and JUnit Vintage (runs JUnit 3/4 tests; deprecated in JUnit 6 and meant only for migrating). Annotations live in `org.junit.jupiter.api`; mixing them with JUnit 4's `org.junit.Test` in one class is a common reason tests are silently not run.

## A test

```java
class ShortestPathTest {
    @Test
    void lineGraphDistance() {
        assertEquals(2, ShortestPath.distance(Graphs.line(3), 0, 2));
    }
}
```

Test classes and methods do not need to be `public` in Jupiter. Static imports from `org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions` provide `assertEquals(expected, actual)`, `assertTrue`, `assertArrayEquals`, `assertIterableEquals`, `assertNull` and `assertAll` for grouped checks. Argument order matters for failure messages: expected first. `assertEquals` on `double` takes a delta.

## Exceptions and timeouts

- `assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> graph.addEdge(-1, 0))` returns the exception so the message can be checked.
- `assertTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1), () -> ...)` fails if the code runs too long, measured after it finishes; `assertTimeoutPreemptively` runs it in another thread and aborts it, which interacts badly with code that depends on thread-local state.

## Lifecycle

`@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach` run around every test; `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` run once per class and must be static unless the class uses `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)`. By default Jupiter creates a new instance of the test class for each test method, so instance fields do not leak between tests.

## Parameterized tests

Requires the `junit-jupiter-params` artifact (included in the `junit-jupiter` aggregate).

```java
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({"0, 0", "1, 1", "10, 55"})
void fibonacci(int n, long expected) { ... }
```

`@ValueSource`, `@MethodSource` (a static factory of `Arguments`), `@EnumSource` and `@NullAndEmptySource` cover other cases. Choose edge cases from the problem constraints: empty, single element, duplicates, extremes, sorted and reverse-sorted input.

## Other features

`@DisplayName`, `@Nested` classes for grouping, `@Disabled` with a reason, `@Tag` for filtering, `@TempDir` for temporary directories, and assumptions (`assumeTrue`) that skip rather than fail.

## Build tools

In JUnit 6 the Platform artifacts share Jupiter's version number, `@CsvSource` parsing uses FastCSV (so messages for malformed rows can differ), and the documentation lives at docs.junit.org. Maven needs Surefire 2.22.0 or later (3.x recommended) to run JUnit Platform tests; Gradle needs `useJUnitPlatform()` in the `test` task. If the build reports zero tests, check the engine dependency and these settings first.

Third-party assertion libraries such as AssertJ and Hamcrest, and mocking with Mockito, are common alongside JUnit but are separate dependencies.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Your build passes but reports 0 tests. Which `@Test` annotation did you import?
- Which inputs from the constraints does your parameterized test leave out?
- Does this field keep its value from one test method to the next?

Java threads, interruption and cancellation

This extends the executor lifecycle starter reference.

## Interruption is a request

Java has no safe way to kill a thread (`Thread.stop` is deprecated and, in recent JDKs, throws `UnsupportedOperationException`). Cancellation is cooperative through the interrupt flag.

- `thread.interrupt()` sets the flag. Blocking methods such as `Thread.sleep`, `Object.wait`, `BlockingQueue.take` and `Future.get` respond by throwing `InterruptedException` and clearing the flag.
- CPU-bound loops must check `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()` themselves.
- Catching `InterruptedException` and doing nothing swallows the request. Either propagate it (declare `throws InterruptedException`) or restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` before returning, so callers can see it.
- `Thread.interrupted()` (static) tests and clears the flag; `isInterrupted()` only tests it.

## Futures and cancellation

`Future.cancel(true)` interrupts the running task if it has started; `cancel(false)` only prevents it from starting. After cancellation, `get()` throws `CancellationException`. A task that ignores interruption keeps running even though its future reports cancelled. `ExecutorService.shutdownNow()` interrupts running tasks in the same way.

## Visibility and the memory model

Without synchronization, a write in one thread may never become visible to another. The Java Memory Model defines "happens-before" edges; the common ones are:

- Unlocking a monitor (`synchronized` exit) or `Lock.unlock` happens before a later lock of the same monitor or lock.
- A write to a `volatile` field happens before a later read of that field.
- `Thread.start` happens before the started thread's actions; a thread's actions happen before another thread returns from `join` on it.
- Actions before submitting a task to an executor happen before the task runs; the task's actions happen before `Future.get` returns.

`volatile` gives visibility and ordering for single reads and writes, but `count++` on a volatile field is still a non-atomic read-modify-write. Use `AtomicInteger`/`LongAdder` or a lock.

## Locks

`synchronized` blocks are reentrant and release automatically on exceptions. `ReentrantLock` adds `tryLock`, timed and interruptible locking; always unlock in `finally`. Acquiring several locks in inconsistent orders can deadlock.

## Virtual threads (Java 21)

Virtual threads (`Thread.ofVirtual()`, `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`) are cheap threads scheduled by the JDK onto a small pool of carrier threads. They suit many concurrent blocking I/O tasks. They do not make CPU-bound work faster, and they do not change the memory model or the need for synchronization. In JDK 21 through 23, blocking inside `synchronized` can pin the carrier thread; JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed most of that pinning. Check the JDK version before advising on it.

Structured concurrency (`StructuredTaskScope`) has been a preview API since JDK 21 and is still in preview in JDK 26 (JEP 525) and JDK 27 (JEP 533). It requires `--enable-preview`, and its API changed between previews.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Your task was cancelled but keeps running. Where does it check for interruption?
- What happens to the interrupt flag in your `catch (InterruptedException e)` block?
- Which happens-before edge makes this field's new value visible to the reader thread?

JavaScript arrays and strings: semantics that affect algorithms

## Arrays are objects with integer-like keys

- `new Array(5)` creates an array of length 5 with five holes (empty slots), not five `undefined` values. `forEach`, `map`, `filter` and `reduce` skip holes; `for...of`, spread and `Array.from` treat them as `undefined`. Create filled arrays explicitly: `new Array(n).fill(0)` or `Array.from({ length: n }, () => 0)`.
- Assigning past the end (`a[100] = 1` on a short array) creates holes and changes `length`.
- `delete a[i]` leaves a hole; use `splice` to remove an element.
- Performance of holey or mixed-type arrays depends on the engine. Engines usually optimize dense arrays of one element kind, but the specification promises nothing about representation or timing. State such claims as engine-specific.

## Shared references in 2-D arrays

`new Array(rows).fill(new Array(cols).fill(0))` fills every row with the same inner array, so writing `grid[0][0]` changes every row. `fill` with an object or array argument inserts that one object everywhere. Build each row separately: `Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(0))`.

## Copying

- `[...a]`, `a.slice()` and `Array.from(a)` make shallow copies: nested arrays and objects are shared.
- `structuredClone(value)` (a host API in modern browsers and Node.js 17+) makes deep copies of plain data; it cannot clone functions or class prototypes.
- JSON round-tripping drops `undefined`, functions and `Map`/`Set`, and fails on `BigInt`.

## Mutating versus copying methods

`push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse` and `fill` mutate the array. `map`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat` and the ES2023 `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with` return new arrays. Mutating an input array inside a function changes the caller's data.

`shift` and `unshift` move every element in the simple model; using `shift` as a queue in a large BFS can be slow. Engines may optimize some cases, so measure; a head index into the array is a portable alternative.

## Strings are UTF-16

- `s.length` counts UTF-16 code units. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, including most emoji, take two units (a surrogate pair).
- `s[i]` and `charCodeAt(i)` return code units; `codePointAt(i)` returns the full code point when `i` is at the start of a pair.
- `for...of` and `[...s]` iterate by code point. Visible "characters" can still be several code points (for example flags or letters with combining marks); `Intl.Segmenter` splits by grapheme clusters.
- Reversing with `s.split("").reverse().join("")` breaks surrogate pairs.
- Strings are immutable. `s[0] = "x"` is silently ignored in sloppy mode and throws a `TypeError` in strict mode (which includes modules and classes). Build a new string, or work on an array of characters and `join` it.

`localeCompare` sorts by locale rules; `<` and the default `sort` compare code units. Pick deliberately.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- You changed one cell and the whole column changed. How many distinct row arrays exist?
- Does `map` visit every index of this array, given how it was created?
- How many code units does each character in your test string use?

JavaScript language versus host environment

ECMAScript defines the language: syntax, types, `Array`, `Map`, `Promise`, `JSON`, `Math`, modules. Everything that touches the outside world comes from the host. Knowing which side an API belongs to explains many "X is not defined" errors.

## Browser host

Provides `window` (also `self`), `document` and the DOM, events, `fetch`, `localStorage`, `setTimeout`, `URL`, `TextEncoder`, Web Workers, `requestAnimationFrame` and many Web APIs. Code runs inside a sandbox with security rules: same-origin policy and CORS for network requests, permission prompts for camera or location, and content security policy set by the page. HTML element behaviour belongs to the HTML standard and DOM, not to JavaScript; see the HTML references for element-level details.

## Node.js host

Provides `process` (arguments, environment, exit codes, stdin/stdout), `Buffer`, modules such as `fs`, `path`, `http`, `crypto`, `child_process`, `worker_threads` and `readline`, and CommonJS `require` alongside ES modules. There is no DOM and no `window`. Node.js has adopted many web APIs as globals (`fetch` in Node.js 18+, `URL`, `TextEncoder`, `AbortController`, `structuredClone`, `performance`), but their availability depends on the Node.js version.

## Portable code

- `globalThis` (ES2020) is the global object in every host.
- `console` is provided by both hosts but is not part of ECMAScript; formatting details differ.
- Check feature availability rather than the host name when possible (`typeof fetch === "function"`).

## Reading input in Node.js (for practice problems)

Online judges and local practice scripts often read stdin. Two common approaches:

- Read everything at once: `require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8")` (file descriptor 0 is stdin), then split on whitespace or lines. Simple and fast for typical inputs.
- Stream lines with the `readline` module (`readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin })`, then `for await (const line of rl)`), which suits large or interactive input.

Input arrives as strings; convert numbers explicitly. Many small `console.log` calls are slow for large outputs; build an array of lines and print `lines.join("\n")` once.

## Exit codes and errors

`process.exitCode = 1` sets the exit status without abruptly stopping pending work; `process.exit()` stops immediately, which can cut off buffered output. Unhandled promise rejections terminate the process by default in Node.js 15 and later.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Is the API that is "not defined" part of JavaScript itself or of a particular host?
- What type is each value you split from stdin?
- How many write calls does your program make for a large output?

JavaScript cancellation with AbortController

Promises have no built-in cancel method. The standard cancellation mechanism in browsers and Node.js is `AbortController` and its `AbortSignal`.

## Basic use

```js
const controller = new AbortController();
const response = fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
// later
controller.abort();
```

- `controller.abort(reason)` marks the signal as aborted, fires its `abort` event once, and records `signal.reason`. Without an argument the reason is a `DOMException` named `AbortError`.
- APIs that accept a signal (`fetch`, `addEventListener`'s `signal` option, many Node.js APIs such as `fs.readFile`, `setTimeout` from `timers/promises`, `events.once`) reject or stop when it aborts. The rejection typically has `name === "AbortError"`, or is the custom reason.
- Aborting is one-way and idempotent: a controller cannot be reset. Create a new one for the next operation.

## Timeouts and combined signals

- `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` returns a signal that aborts with a `TimeoutError` `DOMException` after the delay.
- `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` aborts when any input signal aborts, useful for "user cancel or timeout".

These two static methods arrived later than `AbortController` itself; check the target browsers and Node.js version.

## Supporting cancellation in your own functions

A function that accepts `{ signal }` should:

1. Check `signal?.throwIfAborted()` (or `signal.aborted`) before starting.
2. Listen for `abort` to stop pending work, with `{ once: true }`, and remove the listener when the work finishes so long-lived signals do not accumulate listeners.
3. Check `signal.aborted` between chunks of long work.
4. Reject with `signal.reason` so callers can tell cancellation from failure.

Like other cancellation systems, this is cooperative. Aborting does not stop a synchronous loop that never checks the signal, and it does not undo side effects already performed, such as a server that has already processed the request.

## Handling the rejection

Callers usually treat abort as an expected outcome:

```js
try { await work({ signal }); }
catch (err) { if (err.name !== "AbortError") throw err; }
```

When a custom reason is used, compare against that reason instead.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- What happens to the first request when the user types again and you start a second one?
- Where in your long-running function would an abort actually be noticed?
- How does the caller tell "cancelled" apart from "failed"?

JavaScript scope, closures, this and prototypes

## Scope

- `let` and `const` are block-scoped. Accessing them before the declaration line throws a `ReferenceError` (the temporal dead zone).
- `var` is function-scoped and hoisted with the value `undefined`.
- `const` prevents rebinding the name, not mutation of the object: `const seen = new Set(); seen.add(1)` is fine.

## Closures

A function keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created, by reference. This is how memoized helpers, counters and recursive inner functions keep state.

In a `for (let i = 0; ...)` loop, each iteration gets a fresh binding of `i`, so callbacks created in the loop see different values. With `var i`, all callbacks share one variable and see its final value. A closure keeps everything it references alive, which can retain large arrays longer than expected.

## this depends on how a function is called

- Method call `obj.f()`: `this` is `obj`.
- Plain call `f()`: `this` is `undefined` in strict mode (modules and classes are always strict) and the global object in sloppy mode.
- `f.call(x, ...)`, `f.apply(x, [...])`, `f.bind(x)` set `this` explicitly.
- `new F()` creates a new object as `this`.
- Arrow functions have no own `this`; they use the `this` of the surrounding scope. That makes them good for callbacks inside methods and wrong as object methods that need the object.

Passing `obj.method` as a callback (`arr.forEach(obj.method)`, `setTimeout(obj.method)`) loses `obj`; the method is then called plainly. Bind it, or wrap it in an arrow function.

## Prototypes and classes

Every object has an internal link to a prototype object. Property lookup checks the object, then its prototype, then that object's prototype, up the chain to `null`. Methods defined in a `class` body live on `Class.prototype` and are shared by all instances.

- `class` is syntax over this mechanism, with differences: class bodies are strict, classes must be called with `new`, and class declarations are in the temporal dead zone until evaluated.
- `extends` sets up the chain; a subclass constructor must call `super()` before using `this`.
- `#private` fields (ES2022) are truly private to the class body; `_name` is only a naming convention.
- `Object.create(null)` makes an object with no prototype, so keys such as `"__proto__"` or `"constructor"` cannot collide with inherited properties. For arbitrary keys, `Map` avoids the problem entirely.

## Using objects as dictionaries

Plain objects convert keys to strings (`obj[1]` and `obj["1"]` are the same entry) and inherit properties from `Object.prototype`. `key in obj` checks the chain; `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` (ES2022) checks only own properties. `Map` keeps any value as a key, preserves insertion order and has `size`.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- When your callback runs, what is `this`, given how the callback is invoked?
- How many `i` variables do your timers see?
- Your frequency count reports a key you never inserted. Where did it come from?

JavaScript coercion, equality and truthiness

## Three kinds of equality

- `===` (strict equality) compares without converting types. `NaN === NaN` is false; `0 === -0` is true.
- `==` (loose equality) converts operands first: `"1" == 1`, `0 == ""`, `null == undefined` are all true, while `null == 0` is false. The rules are hard to keep in your head; most style guides use `===` everywhere except `x == null` as a deliberate check for both `null` and `undefined`.
- `Object.is` (SameValue) is like `===` except `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true and `Object.is(0, -0)` is false.

`Map`, `Set` and `Array.prototype.includes` use SameValueZero: like `Object.is` but treating `0` and `-0` as equal. So `[NaN].includes(NaN)` is true, while `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` is -1 because `indexOf` uses `===`.

Objects and arrays are compared by reference: `[1, 2] === [1, 2]` is false, and a `Set` of arrays treats each array as distinct. Encode composite keys (for example `` `${r},${c}` ``) or use nested maps.

## Falsy values

`false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` are falsy; everything else, including `"0"`, `[]` and `{}`, is truthy.

`if (map.get(key))` and `count = count || 1` treat a stored `0` or `""` as missing. Use `map.has(key)`, an explicit comparison, or `??`, which replaces only `null` and `undefined`: `count = count ?? 1`.

## The + operator

If either operand is a string after converting objects to primitives, `+` concatenates: `1 + "2"` is `"12"`, while `"3" - 1` is `2`. Values read from `input` elements, `prompt`, URL parameters and `process.argv` are strings. Convert explicitly with `Number(s)` (strict: `Number("12px")` is NaN, `Number("")` is 0) or `parseInt(s, 10)` (reads a prefix: `parseInt("12px", 10)` is 12).

## Sorting coerces to strings

`array.sort()` without a comparator converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. Pass a comparator: `(a, b) => a - b` for finite numbers. For values where subtraction can overflow or produce NaN, compare explicitly. Since ES2019 `sort` is required to be stable. `toSorted()` (ES2023) returns a sorted copy instead of sorting in place.

## Relational comparison

`<` between two strings compares code units; between a string and a number it converts the string to a number. `"10" < "9"` is true; `"10" < 9` is false. `undefined` converts to NaN, so comparisons with it are always false, which can silently break a "find the maximum" loop that starts from an uninitialized variable.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Which values in your input would make this `if` take the wrong branch?
- What type does this value have when it reaches your addition?
- What comparator does your sort use, and how does it order 10 and 9?

JavaScript event loop and scheduling

This extends the promises and async error-flow starter reference.

## One thread, run to completion

A JavaScript agent runs one piece of code at a time on its thread. Once a function starts, it runs until it returns; nothing else on that thread interrupts it. A long synchronous loop therefore freezes a browser page (no rendering, no input handling) or stalls every request in a Node.js server.

The host (browser or Node.js) owns the event loop: it picks the next task, runs it to completion, then drains the microtask queue, then (in browsers) may render, and repeats.

## Tasks and microtasks

- Tasks (sometimes called macrotasks) include timer callbacks (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`), I/O callbacks, UI events and `MessageChannel` messages.
- Microtasks include promise reactions (`.then`, `.catch`, `.finally`, and the continuation after `await`) and `queueMicrotask` callbacks. After each task, and whenever the JavaScript stack empties, the host runs all queued microtasks, including ones added while draining.

So, given `setTimeout(a, 0); Promise.resolve().then(b); c();`, the order is `c`, then `b`, then `a`. A microtask that keeps scheduling microtasks starves timers and rendering just as a busy loop would.

## Timers are minimums

`setTimeout(fn, ms)` runs `fn` no earlier than `ms` milliseconds later, when the loop gets to it. Browsers clamp nested timers to at least 4 ms after several levels of nesting and throttle timers in background tabs. Timer delays are not a precise clock; use `performance.now()` to measure.

## Node.js specifics

Node.js's loop is implemented by libuv and has phases (timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, close callbacks).

- `setImmediate` callbacks run in the check phase. Whether `setTimeout(fn, 0)` or `setImmediate` runs first from the main module is not deterministic; inside an I/O callback, `setImmediate` runs first.
- `process.nextTick` callbacks run before promise microtasks, after the current operation. Recursive `nextTick` can starve I/O.
- CPU-heavy work belongs in `worker_threads` or a separate process; the libuv thread pool handles some I/O and crypto internally but does not run your JavaScript.

## Browser specifics

`requestAnimationFrame` runs before the next repaint and is the right place for visual updates. Web Workers run JavaScript on separate threads and communicate by messages; they cannot touch the DOM.

## Breaking up long work

For a long algorithm in a UI, split work into chunks and yield between them (for example `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r))`, or `scheduler.yield()` where supported), or move it into a worker. Yielding with a resolved promise does not let rendering or input run, because microtasks drain first.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- In what order do the three logs in your snippet appear, and which queue does each come from?
- Your page freezes while the search runs. When does the browser get a chance to repaint?
- Does `await` on an already-resolved promise let a timer callback run before the next line?

document:
JavaScript numbers and BigInt

## One Number type

Every `number` is an IEEE 754 double-precision float. Integers are exact only up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1 = 9007199254740991). Beyond that, adjacent integers cannot all be represented: `2 ** 53 + 1 === 2 ** 53` is true. `Number.isSafeInteger(x)` checks the range.

Algorithm consequences:

- Products of two values near 10^9 exceed 2^53 and silently lose precision. Modular arithmetic such as `(a * b) % MOD` with `MOD = 1e9 + 7` is wrong when `a * b` is not exact; use `BigInt` for the multiplication or split it.
- Floating-point sums are not exact: `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is false. Compare with a tolerance, or keep values as integers (cents, scaled units).
- `Infinity`, `-Infinity` and `NaN` are numbers. Division by zero gives `Infinity` or NaN rather than throwing. `Number.isNaN` checks for NaN without coercion; global `isNaN` coerces first.

## Integer operations

- There is no integer division operator. `Math.floor(a / b)` floors toward negative infinity; `Math.trunc(a / b)` truncates toward zero. They differ for negative quotients.
- `%` is a remainder with the sign of the dividend: `-7 % 3` is `-1`. Normalize with `((x % m) + m) % m` when a value in `[0, m)` is needed.
- Bitwise operators (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`) convert operands to 32-bit signed integers; `>>>` uses unsigned 32-bit. `x | 0` truncates to 32 bits and wraps large values, so it is not a general "floor". Bitmask DP over more than 31 bits needs `BigInt` or arrays.
- `Math.max()` with no arguments is `-Infinity`; `Math.max(...hugeArray)` can exceed engine argument limits and throw a `RangeError`. Use a loop or `reduce` for large arrays.

## BigInt

`BigInt` (ES2020) holds arbitrary-precision integers: `123n`, `BigInt("9007199254740993")`.

- Mixing `BigInt` and `Number` in arithmetic throws a `TypeError`; convert explicitly. Comparisons (`<`, `==`) between them are allowed.
- Division truncates toward zero; there are no fractions. `>>>` is not supported.
- `Math` functions do not accept `BigInt`.
- `JSON.stringify` throws on `BigInt` values unless a replacer handles them.
- `BigInt` arithmetic is slower than `Number` arithmetic in current engines; use it where exactness requires it.

## Formatting and parsing

`(0.1).toFixed(20)` shows the stored binary approximation. `Number.parseInt` with an explicit radix, and `Number()` for whole strings, are the reliable parsers. `toString(2)` gives binary digits for debugging bit tricks, with a leading `-` for negatives rather than two's complement.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- What is the largest intermediate value in your computation, and is it below 2^53?
- How does your division round when one operand is negative?
- How many bits does your mask need, and how many do JavaScript's bitwise operators keep?

JavaScript packages, module formats and bundlers

This extends the ES modules and resolution starter reference with the tooling around it.

## package.json fields that change how code loads

- `"type": "module"` makes `.js` files in that package ES modules in Node.js; `"type": "commonjs"` (or no field) makes them CommonJS. `.mjs` is always ESM and `.cjs` always CommonJS, regardless of `type`.
- `"exports"` defines the package's public entry points and blocks deep imports of anything not listed. Conditional exports (`"import"`, `"require"`, `"node"`, `"browser"`, `"default"`) choose files by environment. Order of conditions matters: the first match wins.
- `"main"` is the older single entry point, used when `exports` is absent.
- `"imports"` defines private `#name` aliases within the package.
- `dependencies` are needed at run time, `devDependencies` only for development and builds, `peerDependencies` must be provided by the consuming project. A lock file (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`) pins exact resolved versions; commit it for applications.

## CommonJS and ESM interop in Node.js

- ESM can `import` CommonJS modules; the CommonJS `module.exports` becomes the default export, and named exports are detected only when static analysis can find them.
- CommonJS historically could not `require` an ES module and had to use dynamic `import()`, which returns a promise. Newer Node.js releases allow `require()` of synchronous ES modules (no top-level `await`); it is enabled by default from Node.js 22.12 and 20.19. Check the version before relying on it.
- In ESM, `__dirname`, `__filename` and `require` are not defined. Use `import.meta.url` (or `import.meta.dirname`/`import.meta.filename` in recent Node.js releases).
- ESM import specifiers in Node.js need file extensions for relative paths (`./graph.js`), unlike typical bundler setups.

## Bundlers and dev servers

Tools such as Vite, webpack, esbuild and Rollup resolve imports, transform syntax (TypeScript, JSX), and produce files for browsers. They often accept specifiers Node.js would not (extensionless imports, path aliases, CSS imports). Code that works in the bundler can therefore fail under plain Node.js or a test runner with a different resolver. When debugging "module not found", identify which tool resolves the import and check its configuration (for Vite, `resolve.alias`; for TypeScript, `paths` must be mirrored in the bundler).

## Transpile targets

Syntax support differs by browser and Node.js version. Build tools translate newer syntax for older targets (configured by `target` or a Browserslist query), but they do not add missing runtime APIs unless polyfills are included. "Works in dev, breaks in an old browser" usually means a missing polyfill, not a syntax problem.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Is this file loaded as CommonJS or as an ES module, and which setting decides that?
- Which tool resolves this import in development, and which one resolves it in tests?
- Does the package you are importing list this path in its `exports`?

TypeScript conditional and mapped types

These features compute types from other types. They are compile-time only and produce no runtime code.

## keyof and indexed access

- `keyof T` is the union of `T`'s property keys. For a type with a string index signature, `keyof` is `string | number`, because numeric keys are converted to strings in JavaScript.
- `T[K]` is the type of property `K`. `T[number]` gives an array's element type.
- `typeof value` in a type position gives the type of a value, often combined with `as const` to derive a union from a constant list: `typeof DIRECTIONS[number]`.

## Mapped types

```ts
type ReadonlyGrid<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
```

Mapped types iterate over keys. Modifiers `readonly`, `?`, `-readonly` and `-?` add or remove properties' flags. Key remapping with `as` (4.1+) renames or filters keys. The built-in utilities `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick`, `Omit` and `Record` are mapped types. `Record<string, number>` says every string key has a number, which is why reading a missing key is typed as `number` unless `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is on.

## Conditional types

```ts
type ElementOf<T> = T extends readonly (infer U)[] ? U : never;
```

- `T extends U ? X : Y` selects a type.
- `infer` introduces a type variable captured from the matched structure.
- Conditional types distribute over unions when `T` is a naked type parameter: `ElementOf<A | B>` becomes `ElementOf<A> | ElementOf<B>`. Wrap in a tuple (`[T] extends [U]`) to prevent distribution.
- `never` distributes to `never`, which can make an expected result disappear.

Built-ins built this way include `Exclude`, `Extract`, `NonNullable`, `ReturnType`, `Parameters` and `Awaited` (4.5+).

## Template literal types

`` type Cell = `${number},${number}` `` describes strings of that shape at compile time. It does not validate strings created at run time; a `string` from input still needs checking.

## When to stop

Type-level computation can make error messages long and slow the compiler. For learning DSA in TypeScript, plain interfaces, unions and generics cover most needs; reach for conditional types when a library API must express a relationship between input and output types.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- What does your conditional type produce when given a union? Is that what you wanted?
- Which keys does `keyof` produce for a type with an index signature?
- Does this template literal type check the strings your program reads at run time?

document:
TypeScript generics, inference and variance

## Type parameters and constraints

```ts
function maxBy<T>(items: readonly T[], score: (item: T) => number): T | undefined
class MinHeap<T> { constructor(private less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean) {} }
```

`<T extends { id: string }>` constrains `T` so its `id` can be used. `<K extends keyof T>` ties a key parameter to an object type. Generic parameters exist only at compile time; `T` cannot be used as a value (`new T()` is not possible without passing a constructor).

Prefer a comparator or key function parameter to constraining `T` to "comparable": TypeScript's `<` operator accepts `number`, `bigint`, `string` and some other types without a single constraint that means "orderable".

## Inference

TypeScript infers type arguments from the call's arguments.

- Inference picks one candidate per parameter, so `pair(1, "a")` for `<T>(a: T, b: T)` is an error rather than `string | number`, unless both are acceptable as a union in that position.
- Literal types widen: `[1, 2]` is inferred as `number[]`. `as const`, or a `const` type parameter (5.0+), keeps the literal tuple type.
- `NoInfer<T>` (5.4+) stops a parameter position from contributing to inference.
- Inference does not flow backwards from an expected return type in every case. When the result is wrong, write the type argument explicitly.

## Structural typing

Types are compatible when their shapes are compatible, not when they share a declared name. Two unrelated interfaces with the same properties are interchangeable. Object literals passed directly get "excess property" checks; the same object passed through a variable does not.

## Variance

How `Box<Dog>` relates to `Box<Animal>` depends on how `T` is used:

- Read-only positions (return types, `readonly` properties) are covariant.
- Function parameter positions are contravariant under `strictFunctionTypes`, except for parameters of methods declared with method syntax, which stay bivariant for compatibility.
- Mutable arrays are treated covariantly: a `Dog[]` is assignable to `Animal[]`, and pushing a `Cat` through the `Animal[]` alias compiles. This is a known unsoundness. Use `readonly Animal[]` for inputs a function only reads.

TypeScript usually measures variance automatically. Explicit `in`/`out` annotations on type parameters (4.7+) state it for complex types and speed up checking; a wrong annotation is reported.

## Limits worth stating honestly

Deeply recursive generic types can hit instantiation depth limits ("Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite"). Error wording and the exact inference result can change between TypeScript versions; quote the version when explaining a specific diagnostic.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- What type did TypeScript infer for `T` here, and from which argument?
- Your function only reads the array. What does accepting a mutable array allow callers to do?
- Why does this call accept an object that lacks the property you expected to be required?

document:
TypeScript narrowing and discriminated unions

## Narrowing

TypeScript follows control flow and narrows a union type to the members possible on each path:

- `typeof x === "string"`, `x instanceof Map`, `"left" in node`, `Array.isArray(x)`.
- Truthiness (`if (node)`) removes `null` and `undefined`, but also removes `0` and `""` from number and string types at run time, so `if (count)` is the wrong test when 0 is valid.
- Equality: `if (x === null)`, and `x == null` for both `null` and `undefined`.
- Early `return` or `throw` narrows the rest of the function.

Narrowing applies to the variable at that point. It is reset when the value could change, for example after an assignment, inside a callback that runs later, or for a property read through a mutable object between calls.

## Type predicates and assertion functions

- `function isLeaf(n: Node): n is Leaf` narrows at the call site when it returns true. The compiler does not check that the body matches the claim; a wrong predicate silently lies. TypeScript 5.5 can infer predicates for simple functions such as `x => x !== undefined`, which makes `array.filter(...)` narrow element types.
- `function assertDefined<T>(x: T): asserts x is NonNullable<T>` narrows after the call, provided it throws otherwise.

## Discriminated unions

Model states that carry different data with a shared literal field:

```ts
type Result =
  | { kind: "found"; index: number }
  | { kind: "missing" };
```

Checking `r.kind === "found"` narrows `r`, so `r.index` is allowed only in that branch. This is clearer than optional fields such as `{ index?: number }`, where every reader must remember which combinations are valid. Tree and graph code can model nodes this way (`{ kind: "leaf" } | { kind: "inner"; left: Tree; right: Tree }`).

## Exhaustiveness

```ts
switch (r.kind) {
  case "found": ...
  case "missing": ...
  default: {
    const unreachable: never = r; // error if a case is missing
    throw new Error(`unhandled ${String(unreachable)}`);
  }
}
```

Adding a new member to the union then produces a compile error at every switch that does not handle it. With `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` and `noImplicitReturns`, the compiler also reports missing `break` or `return` statements.

## The non-null assertion

`value!` tells the compiler a value is not `null` or `undefined`. It generates no runtime check. If the claim is wrong, the program fails later with a `TypeError` at the use site. Prefer narrowing, or an explicit check that throws with a clear message.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- On this line, which members of the union are still possible?
- What happens at run time if this `!` is wrong?
- If someone adds a new kind of node, which line would tell them they forgot to handle it?

document:
TypeScript at the runtime boundary

## Types are erased

TypeScript checks types and then emits JavaScript with the type annotations removed. At run time there are no interfaces, type aliases or generic arguments. Consequences:

- `JSON.parse`, `fetch(...).json()`, `localStorage`, environment variables and stdin produce data of unknown shape. Annotating the result (`const g: Graph = JSON.parse(text)`) does not check it.
- `x as Graph` is a compile-time assertion only. It suppresses errors; it does not convert or validate.
- `value!` asserts non-null without a check.
- `any` turns checking off and spreads: properties of `any` are `any`. `unknown` is the safe alternative; it forces narrowing before use.

Validate untrusted data with explicit checks or a schema library (for example Zod, Valibot, io-ts, or JSON Schema validators) and derive or check the static type from the same definition.

## TypeScript constructs that do emit code

Most TypeScript syntax is erasable, but a few features generate JavaScript:

- `enum` creates an object. Numeric enums have reverse mappings (`Color[0] === "Red"`) and accept any number when assigned from a `number` in some situations, so they give weaker guarantees than they appear to. String enums have no reverse mapping. `const enum` is inlined, but has pitfalls with isolated per-file compilation.
- `namespace` with values, and constructor parameter properties (`constructor(private x: number)`).
- Legacy experimental decorators with `emitDecoratorMetadata`.

Union-of-literals types (`type Dir = "N" | "E" | "S" | "W"`) with an `as const` array are a common erasable alternative to enums. TypeScript 5.8 added `erasableSyntaxOnly` to reject non-erasable syntax, which matters when running TypeScript through tools that only strip types, such as Node.js's built-in type stripping.

## Assertions versus guarantees

A useful habit when reading or explaining TypeScript code: for each claim, ask whether it is checked by the compiler, checked at run time, or merely asserted.

| Code | Checked by compiler | Checked at run time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `let n: number = f()` | yes, if `f`'s type is accurate | no |
| `data as Graph` | only that the types overlap | no |
| `if (typeof x === "number")` | narrows | yes |
| `isGraph(data)` (type predicate) | trusts the predicate | whatever the body checks |

## Interop with JavaScript libraries

Type declarations (`.d.ts`, bundled with the library or from `@types/*`) describe a JavaScript library's API. They can be out of date or wrong. When behaviour contradicts the types, the JavaScript behaviour is what actually happens.

## Recursion and numbers

TypeScript adds no runtime limits or numeric types: recursion depth, `number` precision and `bigint` behave exactly as in the JavaScript engine that runs the output. See the JavaScript numbers reference.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Which part of this code actually checks that the parsed data has a `nodes` array?
- What does this `as` assertion do when the program runs?
- What values can this numeric enum variable hold at run time?

document:
TypeScript tsconfig.json

`tsconfig.json` marks a TypeScript project root and configures the compiler (`tsc`) and editors. Running `tsc` with no file arguments uses it; passing files on the command line ignores it. Diagnostics differ under different settings, so when explaining an error, check which options are on.

## Which files

`include`, `exclude` and `files` choose the inputs; `extends` inherits a base config (for example from the `@tsconfig/*` packages); `references` with `composite: true` split a large codebase into projects built with `tsc -b`.

## Strictness

`"strict": true` turns on a family of checks, including:

- `strictNullChecks`: `null` and `undefined` are separate types and must be handled. Without it, any value may silently be null.
- `noImplicitAny`: parameters and variables with no inferable type are errors instead of `any`.
- `strictFunctionTypes`: function parameter types are checked contravariantly (method-style declarations are still checked bivariantly).
- `strictPropertyInitialization`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables` (catch variables are `unknown`), `alwaysStrict` and others.

From TypeScript 6.0, `strict` is on by default; in 5.x it has to be set. New checks are sometimes added to the `strict` family in new TypeScript releases, so upgrading can produce new errors. Additional, separate flags are useful for algorithm code:

- `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`: `arr[i]` and `record[key]` include `undefined` in their type, which matches what actually happens out of bounds.
- `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noImplicitReturns`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`.

## Output

- `target` sets which JavaScript syntax is emitted (for example `ES2022`). Newer syntax is downleveled for older targets. `target` does not add runtime APIs.
- `lib` sets which built-in type declarations exist (`ES2023`, `DOM`). If `Array.prototype.toSorted` is reported missing, the `lib` (or `target`, which implies a default `lib`) is older than the API.
- `outDir`, `rootDir`, `sourceMap`, `declaration` (emit `.d.ts`), `noEmit` (type-check only, when another tool such as esbuild, swc or Vite produces the JavaScript).

## Modules

- `module` controls the emitted module format and how imports are interpreted: `nodenext` (or `node16`/`node18`) to model Node.js's ESM/CommonJS rules, `preserve` or `esnext` when a bundler handles output.
- `moduleResolution`: `nodenext` for Node.js, `bundler` (5.0+) for bundlers that allow extensionless imports.
- `verbatimModuleSyntax` (5.0+) keeps imports exactly as written, so type-only imports must use `import type`.
- `paths` and `baseUrl` affect type-checking only; the runtime or bundler must be configured with the same aliases. `baseUrl` is deprecated from TypeScript 6.0.
- `esModuleInterop` and `allowSyntheticDefaultImports` affect default imports from CommonJS modules.

## TypeScript 6.0 changes

C++ comparators and ordering

## The Compare requirement

`std::sort`, `std::set`, `std::map`, `std::priority_queue`, `std::lower_bound` and related algorithms require a comparator `comp(a, b)` that imposes a strict weak ordering:

- Irreflexive: `comp(a, a)` is false.
- Asymmetric: if `comp(a, b)` then not `comp(b, a)`.
- Transitive, and equivalence (neither `comp(a, b)` nor `comp(b, a)`) is transitive.

Violating it is undefined behaviour. A comparator written with `<=` breaks irreflexivity; with some standard library implementations, `std::sort` can then read outside the range and crash. Comparators that look at floating-point values containing NaN break transitivity. Debug modes of the standard libraries can check some of this.

## Common comparator shapes

- Sort by several keys: `return std::tie(a.cost, a.id) < std::tie(b.cost, b.id);` gives lexicographic order.
- C++20 `operator<=>` can be defaulted (`auto operator<=>(const Edge&) const = default;`) to compare members in declaration order, and also generates `==` when defaulted.
- Avoid subtraction-based comparisons (`a - b < 0`): they overflow and are not needed in C++.

## Equivalence is the key in ordered containers

`std::set` and `std::map` treat two keys as the same if neither compares less than the other. A comparator on only one field silently merges distinct elements that tie on it. Add tie-breakers when distinct elements must be kept, or use `multiset`.

## Sorting

`std::sort` is not stable and is O(n log n) comparisons (guaranteed since C++11). `std::stable_sort` keeps equal elements in order. `std::partial_sort` and `std::nth_element` are cheaper when you only need the top k or the k-th element.

## priority_queue

`std::priority_queue<T>` with the default `std::less<T>` is a max-heap: `top()` is the largest element. For a min-heap, use `std::priority_queue<T, std::vector<T>, std::greater<T>>`, or invert a custom comparator. The comparator is "less" in heap order, which is the opposite of what many learners expect when writing a lambda for a min-heap. There is no decrease-key or iteration; Dijkstra-style code pushes duplicates and skips stale entries.

## Hashing for unordered containers

`std::unordered_map` and `std::unordered_set` need `std::hash<Key>` and `==`. The standard library does not provide `std::hash` for `std::pair` or `std::tuple`. Options: encode the pair into one integer (for example `(uint64_t)r << 32 | c` for non-negative 32-bit values), provide a custom hasher type as a template argument, or specialize `std::hash` for your own type. A poor hash function makes operations degrade towards linear time; average constant time assumes a good hash.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- What does your comparator return when both arguments are the same element?
- Your set has fewer elements than you inserted. Which pairs does your comparator consider equivalent?
- Which element does `top()` return with the comparator you passed?

C++ copy and move semantics

## Copies are the default

Assigning, passing by value or returning a class object copies it unless a move or elision applies. Copying a `std::vector<int>` of a million elements copies a million ints. Passing containers by value to recursive functions is a common accidental O(n) per call. Take `const std::vector<int>&` for read-only parameters.

## Moves transfer resources

A move constructor or move assignment takes an rvalue reference (`T&&`) and steals the source's resources, leaving it in a "valid but unspecified state". For standard library types, that means the object can be destroyed or assigned to, but its value should not be relied on (a moved-from `vector` is often empty, but that is not guaranteed for every type).

`std::move(x)` does not move anything. It is a cast to an rvalue that allows a move overload to be chosen. After `v2 = std::move(v1)`, using `v1`'s contents is a bug.

## When moves happen automatically

- Returning a local object by value: since C++17, returning a prvalue (`return T(...)`) is guaranteed not to copy or move. Returning a named local (`return result;`) is usually elided (NRVO) and otherwise moved. Writing `return std::move(result);` can prevent elision; compilers warn about it (`-Wpessimizing-move`).
- Temporaries bind to `T&&` overloads: `v.push_back(std::string("x"))` moves.
- `emplace_back(args...)` constructs in place, avoiding a temporary.

## noexcept matters for containers

When a `vector` reallocates, it moves elements to new storage only if the move constructor is `noexcept` (or the type is not copyable); otherwise it copies, to keep the strong exception guarantee (`std::move_if_noexcept`). A user-defined type with a throwing or non-`noexcept` move constructor therefore makes `vector` growth copy every element. Defaulted move constructors are `noexcept` when all members' moves are.

## Which special members the compiler generates

- Declaring a copy operation or destructor suppresses the implicit move operations; the class then copies where it could have moved.
- Declaring a move operation deletes the implicit copy operations.
- Following the rule of zero (let members manage resources) avoids most of these traps; see the lifetime and RAII reference.

## References and views

- `const T&` parameters bind to temporaries and extend nothing beyond the call.
- `std::string_view` (C++17) and `std::span` (C++20) are non-owning views. Returning a `string_view` into a local `std::string`, or storing one that refers to a temporary string, dangles. A view is valid only while the viewed data is alive and unmodified in ways that reallocate.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- How many times is this vector copied during the recursion?
- What does your code assume about `v1` after it was moved from?
- Is your type's move constructor `noexcept`, and what does `vector` do when it is not?

document:
C++ exception safety

## The guarantees

Library documentation and code reviews describe what an operation promises if it throws:

- No-throw (nothrow): the operation never throws. Destructors, `swap`, and move operations should be in this category, and are marked `noexcept`.
- Strong: if it throws, the program state is as if the call never happened (commit or roll back).
- Basic: if it throws, no resources leak and all objects remain in a valid but possibly changed state.
- None: anything can happen. Avoid.

Examples from the standard library: `vector::push_back` provides the strong guarantee if the element's copy or `noexcept` move constructor is used for reallocation; `std::sort` provides the basic guarantee if the comparator or swaps throw.

## How to get the strong guarantee

Do all the work that can fail on the side, then commit with operations that cannot fail. The copy-and-swap idiom builds a new copy and then swaps it in with a non-throwing `swap`. The same idea applies to C structures (see the C adjacency-list reference): allocate everything first, then link.

## noexcept

A function marked `noexcept` that lets an exception escape calls `std::terminate`. Mark moves, destructors and `swap` as `noexcept` when they cannot throw: containers use that to choose moves over copies. Destructors are implicitly `noexcept` unless declared otherwise; throwing from a destructor during stack unwinding terminates the program.

## Catching

- Throw by value, catch by reference: `catch (const std::exception& e)`. Catching by value slices derived exceptions.
- `throw;` rethrows the current exception unchanged.
- Standard exceptions used in DSA code: `std::out_of_range` from `vector::at` and `map::at`, `std::bad_alloc` when allocation fails, `std::length_error`, `std::invalid_argument` from `std::stoi`. `operator[]` on `vector` does not check bounds; out-of-range access is undefined behaviour, not an exception. `map::operator[]` inserts a default value for a missing key, which also means it cannot be used on a `const map`.

## Alternatives to exceptions

- Return `std::optional<T>` (C++17) for "maybe a value".
- Return `std::expected<T, E>` (C++23) to carry an error value without exceptions. Library support depends on the compiler and standard library version.
- Some codebases (games, embedded, parts of large companies) compile with exceptions disabled (`-fno-exceptions`); then the standard library's throwing paths typically abort instead.

## Stack overflow is not an exception

Deep recursion that exhausts the stack is undefined behaviour in C++ and usually crashes the process. There is no portable way to catch it. The depth limit depends on the platform's stack size and frame sizes.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- If this allocation throws halfway through your insert, what state is the structure left in?
- Does `operator[]` here check the index? What does `at` do differently?
- Why does `map[key]` fail to compile on your `const` reference?

C++ iterator invalidation

An iterator, pointer or reference into a container is invalidated when the operation that changed the container is allowed to move or destroy the element it refers to. Using an invalidated iterator is undefined behaviour: it may appear to work, crash, or corrupt data.

## Summary table (standard guarantees)

| Container | Insertion | Erasure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vector` | If the new size exceeds `capacity()`, reallocation invalidates all iterators, pointers and references. Otherwise those before the insertion point stay valid; those at or after it, and `end()`, are invalidated. | Iterators and references at or after the erased position, including `end()`, are invalidated. |
| `deque` | Insert at either end invalidates all iterators but keeps references and pointers to elements valid. Insert in the middle invalidates all iterators and references. | Erasing the first or last element invalidates only iterators and references to the erased element (erasing the last also invalidates `end()`). Erasing in the middle invalidates all. |
| `list`, `forward_list` | No invalidation. | Only the erased elements. |
| `map`, `set`, `multimap`, `multiset` | No invalidation. | Only the erased elements. |
| `unordered_map`, `unordered_set` and multi versions | If the insertion causes a rehash, all iterators are invalidated, but pointers and references to elements stay valid. Without a rehash, nothing is invalidated. | Only the erased elements. |

`vector::reserve` and `shrink_to_fit` invalidate everything when they reallocate. `clear` invalidates all iterators into the container. `std::string` behaves like `vector` for reallocation, and any modifying operation can invalidate pointers returned by `data()` or `c_str()`.

## Patterns that break

- Range-based `for (auto& x : v)` while calling `v.push_back(...)` inside the loop. The loop holds iterators that reallocation invalidates.
- Storing `&v[i]` or `v.begin() + i` in another structure (for example a graph node pointing at elements of a `vector<Node>`) and then adding elements. Store indices instead, or reserve the final size up front and never exceed it.
- Erasing inside a loop with `++it` after `erase(it)`.

## Patterns that work

- Use the iterator returned by `erase`: `it = v.erase(it);` and only increment when not erasing. The same pattern works for `list`, `map` and `unordered_map` (whose `erase` also returns the next iterator since C++11).
- For removing many elements: the erase-remove idiom `v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred), v.end());`, or C++20 `std::erase_if(v, pred)`, which also works for associative and unordered containers.
- Collect changes and apply them after the loop.

## Detecting it

Debug modes catch many invalidation bugs at run time: libstdc++ debug mode (`-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG`), libc++ hardening modes, and MSVC's debug iterators (`_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL`). AddressSanitizer reports uses of freed vector storage. These checks slow programs down and are for testing.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Did the vector's capacity change between the moment you took this pointer and the moment you used it?
- After `erase`, which iterator does your loop move to next?
- Your graph stores pointers to nodes inside a vector. What happens to them when you add a node?

C++ object lifetime, RAII and smart pointers

## Lifetime

Every object has a lifetime that starts when its initialization completes and ends when its destructor starts (or when its storage is reused). Automatic (local) objects are destroyed at the end of their scope, in reverse order of construction. Members are destroyed after the class's destructor body runs, in reverse declaration order. Temporaries usually die at the end of the full expression that created them.

Using an object after its lifetime ends is undefined behaviour. The common forms are returning a reference or pointer to a local, keeping a reference into a container that reallocates (see the iterator invalidation reference), and lambdas or views that outlive what they refer to.

## RAII

Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: tie each resource (memory, file, lock, socket) to an object whose constructor acquires it and whose destructor releases it. Because destructors run during normal scope exit and during stack unwinding from an exception, the resource is released on every path.

Standard examples: `std::vector` and `std::string` own their memory; `std::fstream` closes its file; `std::lock_guard` and `std::scoped_lock` release mutexes; `std::unique_ptr` deletes its object.

## Smart pointers

- `std::unique_ptr<T>`: sole ownership, movable but not copyable, no overhead beyond a raw pointer with the default deleter. Create with `std::make_unique<T>(args)` (C++14). It is the default choice for tree nodes and owned polymorphic objects.
- `std::shared_ptr<T>`: shared ownership with an atomic reference count. Create with `std::make_shared`. The object is destroyed when the last owner goes away. Reference cycles (parent and child both holding `shared_ptr` to each other) are never freed; break them with `std::weak_ptr` for back-pointers.
- Raw pointers and references for non-owning access: a function that only reads a node takes `const Node&` or `const Node*`, not a smart pointer.

## Trees and recursion in destructors

A linked list or a degenerate tree built from `unique_ptr<Node> next` frees itself recursively: destroying the head destroys the next node, and so on. For very long chains this recursion can overflow the stack. The depth at which that happens depends on the platform and stack size. Long lists may need a destructor that unlinks nodes iteratively.

## The rule of zero, three and five

- Rule of zero: if members manage their own resources (`vector`, `unique_ptr`, `string`), do not write a destructor, copy or move operations; the defaults are correct.
- Rule of three/five: a class that manages a raw resource directly needs a destructor, copy constructor and copy assignment (and move constructor and move assignment), or must delete the ones it cannot support. See the copy and move reference.

## Containers own their elements

`std::vector<Node>` owns `Node` objects by value; erasing an element destroys it. `std::vector<Node*>` owns only the pointers, so the nodes must be freed elsewhere. `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>>` owns the nodes and keeps their addresses stable when the vector grows.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Which object owns this node, and when is it destroyed?
- If an exception is thrown on this line, which resources are released and by whom?
- These two nodes point at each other with `shared_ptr`. What is each one's reference count when the rest of the program lets go of them?

C++ standard versions, build flags and diagnostics

A C++ answer is only correct relative to a standard version and a toolchain. Ask which standard the learner compiles with (`-std=c++17`, `-std=c++20`, `/std:c++20`) before suggesting library features. Compilers may support a language feature before their standard library ships the matching header, so check both.

## Features by standard (selected, DSA-relevant)

C++17:
- Structured bindings: `for (auto& [key, count] : freq)`.
- `std::optional`, `std::variant`, `std::string_view`.
- `if constexpr`, class template argument deduction, `if (init; cond)`.
- `std::gcd`, `std::lcm` in `<numeric>`; `std::clamp`.
- Parallel algorithm overloads (`std::execution::par`), with uneven library support.

C++20:
- Concepts and `requires`; ranges (`std::ranges::sort(v)`, views such as `std::views::filter`, `iota`, `reverse`).
- `std::span`; `std::format` (library support arrived later than compiler support in some toolchains).
- Three-way comparison `<=>` and defaulted comparisons.
- `contains()` on associative containers; `std::erase_if`; `std::midpoint`; `<bit>` (`std::popcount`, `std::countl_zero`, `std::bit_width`).
- Designated initializers, coroutines, modules (tooling support still uneven).

C++23:
- `std::print` / `std::println`, `std::expected`, `std::flat_map`/`std::flat_set`, `std::mdspan`.
- `std::ranges::to<std::vector>()`, `views::zip`, `views::enumerate`, `views::chunk`.
- Explicit object parameters ("deducing this"), multidimensional subscript operator, `std::generator`.

## Warning and checking flags (GCC/Clang)

- `-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic` for common problems; `-Wshadow` and `-Wconversion` for shadowed names and narrowing conversions.
- `-fsanitize=address,undefined` to catch out-of-bounds access, use-after-free and signed overflow on executed paths.
- Standard library checking: libstdc++ `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` (cheap bounds checks on `operator[]` and others) or `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` (full debug mode, changes the ABI, so all code must be built with it); libc++ hardening modes set through `_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE`; MSVC debug builds check iterators by default.
- `-O2` for timing; `-O0 -g` for debugging. A bug that only appears with optimization is often undefined behaviour, not a compiler bug.

## Reading common errors

- "no match for operator<" in a `std::set` or `std::sort` instantiation: the element type has no ordering; add a comparator or `operator<=>`.
- "use of deleted function" when copying: the type is move-only (for example it holds a `unique_ptr`); move it or pass by reference.
- "call to implicitly-deleted default constructor": a member lacks a default constructor.
- "undefined reference" at link time for a template: its definition is not visible where it is used.
- Long template backtraces: find the first "required from here" in your own file.

## The One Definition Rule

Non-inline functions and variables must be defined once across the program. Defining a non-inline function in a header included by two `.cpp` files breaks the rule; mark it `inline` (implicit for templates, member functions defined in the class, and `constexpr` functions) or move the definition into one source file. Some ODR violations are not diagnosed and lead to inconsistent behaviour.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Which `-std` flag does your build use, and is the header you included available in that standard library version?
- What do the sanitizers report when you run the failing test?
- Is this an error from the compiler or from the linker?

C++ templates, concepts and lambdas

## Templates

A function or class template is a pattern the compiler instantiates for each set of template arguments used. Consequences:

- Template definitions must be visible where they are used, so they normally live in headers. Defining a template in a `.cpp` file and using it from another file produces "undefined reference" linker errors unless it is explicitly instantiated.
- Errors in template code appear at instantiation and can be long. Read the first error and the "required from here" line that points into your own code.
- `if constexpr` (C++17) discards branches that do not apply to a given type.
- Class template argument deduction (CTAD, C++17) lets you write `std::pair p{1, 2.0};` or `std::vector v{1, 2, 3};`.

## Concepts (C++20)

Concepts name requirements on template arguments and give earlier, shorter errors:

```cpp
template <std::totally_ordered T>
T max_of(const std::vector<T>& v);

auto sum(std::ranges::input_range auto&& r);
```

Standard concepts live in `<concepts>` and `<iterator>`/`<ranges>`: `std::integral`, `std::floating_point`, `std::totally_ordered`, `std::invocable`, `std::ranges::random_access_range` and more. A `requires` clause or expression states custom requirements. Concepts check syntax (that expressions compile), not semantics: `std::totally_ordered` cannot verify that `<` is actually a strict ordering.

## Lambdas

- Capture by value `[x]` copies at creation time; capture by reference `[&x]` refers to the variable, which must outlive the lambda. Storing a lambda that captured locals by reference (in a callback, a thread or a returned `std::function`) and calling it after the function returned is undefined behaviour.
- `[=]` and `[&]` capture everything used. In member functions, `[=]` implicitly capturing `this` is deprecated in C++20; write `[this]` or `[*this]`.
- Generic lambdas (C++14) take `auto` parameters; C++20 allows an explicit template parameter list: `[]<typename T>(const std::vector<T>& v) { ... }`.
- A lambda captured state is `const` inside the call unless the lambda is `mutable`.

## Recursive lambdas

A lambda cannot refer to itself by name in its own initializer. Options:

- `std::function<int(int)> dfs = [&](int u) { ... dfs(v) ... };` works but adds type erasure and possible allocation; it is usually slower than a plain function.
- Pass the lambda to itself: `auto dfs = [&](auto&& self, int u) -> void { ... self(self, v); };` then call `dfs(dfs, root)`.
- C++23 explicit object parameter ("deducing this"): `auto dfs = [&](this auto&& self, int u) -> void { ... self(v); };`. Requires compiler support for C++23: GCC 13 rejects it even with `-std=c++23` (checked 2026-10-18), and GCC added it in version 14. Check the learner's compiler before suggesting this form.
- Or write an ordinary function or a small struct with a member function.

Deep recursion through any of these has the same stack limits as ordinary recursion.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)

- Which line in the compiler output points into your code rather than into the library?
- Does the variable this lambda captured by reference still exist when the lambda runs?
- Which C++ standard is your compiler using, and does it support the recursive lambda form you wrote?
